article_text:
Elsinore

This film puts Andrew Scott in line to become the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar . He plays Ian Charleson, who became a star in Chariots of Fire and in 1989 took on the role of Hamlet at London’s National Theatre when Daniel Day-Lewis withdrew, despite being desperately ill with Aids, knowing that the strain would accelerate his illness. For Charleson, the play’s themes of life and death, truth and falsehood, justice and injustice, were all too real.

7 Miles Out

Fans of Manchester, Manchesterism and indie British film-maker Carol Morley will relish the thought of her much anticipated new movie, adapted from her autobiographical novel of the same title. The lead character, Ann, based on Morley herself, experiences an emotional crisis as a teen and takes refuge in the thrilling new Manchester music scene, featuring bands including Joy Division, New Order and Magazine. Lucy Halliday is Ann and her mum and dad are played by Gemma Whelan and Aidan Gillen.

Fatherland

Polish film-maker Paweł Pawlikowski has created a brilliantly poised, superbly performed historical vignette in black-and-white whose brevity and control can hardly contain its characters’ anguish. Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller play Thomas and Erika Mann – that is, the great Nobel-winning German author and his daughter. After the war and the destruction of the Nazis, whose tyranny he escaped by fleeing to the US, Mann returns to Germany with daughter in tow, to accept prizes in the fatherland’s capitalist West and communist East. But he is in denial about a terrible family crisis.

La Gradiva

Surely the year’s best debut feature? French cinematographer turned director Marine Atlan tells a gripping story of a school trip to Pompeii: an emotionally troubled teacher has to keep an emotionally troubled bunch of kids in line. Perhaps the most difficult is a boy called Toni, who has always believed a story told him by his mum that he has aristocratic lineage from a Pompeii nobleman whose castle was reduced to rubble by southern Italy’s 1980 earthquake, an event he thinks is thrillingly analogous to the Pompeii disaster. He’s heading for his own emotional earthquake.

I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning

Birmingham is the setting for this absorbing and moving social realist picture from film-maker Clio Barnard , featuring terrific performances from its young cast. It’s a home town drama about a city to which the characters are fundamentally loyal while simultaneously longing to escape; as they approach the end of their 20s, they must come to terms with decisions and life choices. Joe Cole, Daryl McCormack, Lola Petticrew, Anthony Boyle and Jay Lycurgo are the cast-members bursting with energy, tenderness and vulnerability.

A Long Winter

Andrew Haigh’s mysterious and beautiful new film is adapted by him from a story by Colm Tóibín: a poignant, subversive study of grief and desire, and the terrible, infantilised loneliness of men without women. A family living a tough existence in remote 1950s Colorado are traumatised when the troubled mother of the household, played by Caitriona Balfe, disappears one winter and the menfolk, having decided that the search can only resume once the snows have melted, enter into a strange new period of bachelor freedom.

The Blood Countess

It’s the part she was born to play. Isabelle Huppert is Countess Elizabeth Báthory, a 16th-century Hungarian noblewoman and serial killer, legendary for having the blood of hundreds of young girls on her hands, and indeed all over the rest of her body, in an attempt to attain eternal youth. Her Báthory is a vampire who has returned to present-day Vienna, the historical seat of the Austro-Hungarian empire, seen initially gliding through its sewers as if on a royal barge, making her way far more coolly than Harry Lime in The Third Man.

I Love Boosters

Chicago rapper and film-maker Boots Riley , the comic bard of black anxiety and white privilege, returns with a hyperactive romp about a bandit group of fashion influencers who deal with the issue of price by simply “boosting” clothes from stores. This group of outlaws includes Naomi Ackie and Taylour Paige, and the resentful fashionista ice-queen whose wares are being sticky-fingered in this way is played by Demi Moore.

Gentle Monster

Here is a coldly eloquent and disquieting drama starring Léa Seydoux about women who find themselves imprisoned by a duty of care and loyalty to the men in their lives. Seydoux plays Lucy, an acclaimed musician with a TV director husband and three-year-old child; one day, the police show up at their door to take away the husband’s computers, tablets and smartphones. The husband replies unconvincingly to Lucy’s desperate questions as to what this is all about, and her ordeal is her need to believe him, to twist and contort what she sees so it will fit into the husband’s shapeshifting explanations.

The Debut

Jesse Eisenberg follows up his excellent drama A Real Pain with this much admired and widely enjoyed dramedy about community theatre, for which Julianne Moore may be once again in the Oscar conversation. She plays a neglected housewife, going mad with boredom and emotional neglect in her Stepford prison; she tries out for a local amateur troupe’s production of a musical (whose hokey songs Eisenberg has himself written). Needless to say, she transforms from a suburban doormat into a Bette Davis-level diva.

My Notes on Mars

Hungarian film-maker Lili Horvát has always had a taste for the inexplicable; now she makes her English-language debut with a film that fuses romance, science fiction and mystery. Mackenzie Davis is Margot, a scientist with emotional problems who vanishes while on a hiking trip with her husband Sam, played by Rupert Friend. Much later, at her memorial service, Margot sensationally reappears, with no memory of what happened, but a determination to destroy her notes on Mars. Is that where’s she’s … gulp … been?

Tender Loving Care

Is this Mike Leigh’s final film ? Let’s hope not. It’s a tender, poignant drama that is also candid and forthright, muscular in its effects. It’s an intergenerational story about the friendship of two women from west London, Rosie and Amy, who share a flat and work in social care. The film gives a complex, interrelated pattern of scenes showing their personal and professional lives and the people close to them. It is a lovely film.

article_text:
K iri is a lively yellow dinosaur, Lou is an amiable purple palorchecie (a fictional beast, vaguely resembling a palorchestes , which in turn vaguely resembles a giant tapir) – and if you’ve been watching their CBeebies show, which hails from New Zealand and consists of 5-minute episodes, you’ll know they’re the best of friends despite their ingrained temperamental differences. But how did they become friends in the first place? For the uninitiated, Kiri and Lou Go Raaa! functions as an introduction to the characters and their world, while for fans it’s a delightful origin story.

At only one hour long, the runtime is toddler-friendly – and to be honest, there are plenty of films marketed at adults that could learn a lesson from writer-director Harry Sinclair’s economical storytelling. (Sinclair is also the writer of the TV series, alongside Buffy the Vampire Slayer writing alum Rebecca Kirshner.) With the voice acting talents of Olivia Tennet (Freda in Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers) and Jemaine Clement (Flight of the Conchords), plus dreamy songs from Don McGlashan (Blam Blam Blam, The Front Lawn), Kiri and Lou Go Raaa! would arguably work superbly as an audiobook or radio show – except the visuals are a treat too.

It’s a cliche to bang on about the fingerprints in the modelling clay, as if effort and a handmade aesthetic automatically equate to great storytelling, but in this case, the tactile quality of the animation does help underscore the gentle perils of the duo’s various adventures. There’s the sense that they aren’t just computer sprites existing in some nebulous cloud, ergo they actually could be washed away in the sea, or melted by a “smoky mountain”. And there’s a wholesomeness to stop-motion that’s hard to beat; it’s a tangible reminder of the physical world, outside screens and digital ephemera. Co-director Anthony Elworthy’s long list of credits, including The Boxtrolls, My Life as a Courgette and Kubo and the Two Strings, also functions as a whistle-stop tour of some of the best children’s animation of the last decade-plus, so perhaps it shouldn’t be a surprise that this big-screen adventure has turned out so beautifully.

article_text:
The IDA Documentary Awards announced its shortlists of the year’s top documentaries Tuesday, boosting Oscar prospects for a select group of feature films and shorts.

Some of the most touted documentaries of the year made the cut, but the list is equally newsworthy for what got left out. In the features categories, 16 films will compete for Best Documentary at the awards show set for December 4 in Los Angeles, among them: A Fox Under a Pink Moon , A Life Illuminated , Birds of War , Nuestra Tierra , Nuisance Bear , One in a Million , and You Can See Everything – the Elizabeth Holmes documentary that has become a runaway box office hit .

Related Stories

International Documentary Association Calls On Israeli Government To Halt "Campaign Of Threats" Against 'NAZA' Directors

IDA Announces Getting Real '26 Lineup, Including "Conversations Usually Too Risky Or Raw To Have Anywhere Else"

Also making the list – Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile , the follow up to her Oscar-shortlisted My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow . Two-time Oscar winner Ben Proudfoot earned a spot on the list with his feature The Eyes of Ghana , and Pegah Ahangarani’s Rehearsals for a Revolution , winner of the L’Oeil d’or prize at Cannes, also made the list.

Watch on Deadline

But there were some shocking snubs in that category: no love for Musk , 14 th , nor two prominent Gaza-themed films – American Doctor and NAZA . Also missing out was Once Upon a Time in Harlem , one of the most honored documentaries of the year. The shortlist selection committee favored some comparatively obscure titles, like Concrete Land , directed by Asmahan Bkerat; Filthy , directed by Bàrbara Mestanza and Marc Pujolar; Silver , directed by Natalia Koniarz, and The Fabulous Time Machine , directed by Eliza Capai.

Scroll for the complete lists.

On the shortlist of short films, a dozen documentaries made the cut, including They’re Here , directed by Oscar winner Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller. That timely documentary, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival, examines the deadly ICE occupation of Minneapolis, MN. Bill Morrison, Oscar-nominated last year for Incident , made the list with his latest short, Sawyer Avenue, Sunday Afternoon . That documentary also centers on ICE, in this case, the seizure of a man by federal agents “without a warrant on a residential street in Chicago.”

Remarkably, four New York Times Op-Docs films made the shorts shortlist: A Wolf in the Suburbs , directed by Amélie Hardy; Sanyi Kakas (Sanyi the Rooster) , directed by Lotte Salomons; Son , directed by Leona Cauklija, and Stalin Boys , directed by Bianca Giaever and Ora DeKornfeld.

Director Yoruba Richen also made the shorts shortlist with Free Joan Little , as did Oscar-nominated filmmaker Waad Al-Kateab with Maybe Tomorrow , co-directed with Wafa Mustafa. But in a surprise, two-time Oscar nominee Joshua Oppenheimer didn’t get recognized for his new short, The Revolution Against Death (recently acquired by the New York Times Op-Docs ).

The 42 nd IDA Documentary Awards will be presented on Friday, December 4 at The Ebell of Los Angeles. Tabitha Jackson, director of Film Forum in New York City and former director of the Sundance Film Festival, will host the ceremony. In a release, the nonprofit IDA said, “At a time when filmmakers face critical distribution and funding challenges, IDA looks forward to gathering and uplifting this irrepressible global community and introducing their work to new audiences.”

The five nominees for the Best Feature and Best Short categories will be selected from the shortlists that were revealed Tuesday, with nominations set to be announced on November 17. “IDA members from 100 countries will view and vote for the Best Feature and Best Short category winners until voting closes on November 29.”

Additional IDA Awards will be presented in the following categories with winners selected by jurors consisting of 200+ documentary professionals from 60+ countries: Best Director, Best Cinematography, Best Editing, Best Original Music Score, Best Production, Best Sound Design, Best Writing, Best Curated Series, Best Episodic Series, Best Documentary Not in the English Language, Best Music Documentary, Best Student Documentary Award, the ABC News VideoSource Award, and the Pare Lorentz Award.

These are the films that made the shortlists announced Tuesday:

Best Feature Documentary Shortlist

In alphabetical order by film title.

article_text:
Joël Andrianomearisoa Kudzanai Chiurai Salah Elmur Frances Goodman Tayie Idahor Isaac Julien Glenn Ligon Thebetsile Magugu Michele Mathison Misheck Masamvu Nandipha Mntambo Daniella Mooney Zanele Muholi Ebony G. Patterson Jody Paulsen Thania Petersen Athi-Patra Ruga Brett Charles Seiler Banele Khoza

The Zeitz MOCAA Permanent Collection was established in 2015 and is focused on contemporary artistic practices from Africa and its global diaspora. It consists of over 500 objects, ranging from works on paper and canvas, photographic prints, sculptures, video works, installations and more. Featuring artists from multiple countries, including South Africa, Zimbabwe, Nigeria, Madagascar, the United States, Kenya, and Sudan, the collection is a rich testament to the diversity of contemporary practices from the continent and beyond.

A large part of the collection consists of a recent donation of artworks which were formerly on a long-term loan from art collector, and co-founder of the museum, Jochen Zeitz. Other works have been gifted to the museum by artists, collectors, and art enthusiasts.

Our collection is thoroughly contemporary and addresses several relevant discourses in Africa and the world today, like migration, human rights, visibility, memory, and desire. Notably, it includes works by some of the most celebrated artists working in the world today. We also hold comprehensive bodies of work from singular artists like Nandipha Mntambo, Zanele Muholi and Kudzanai Chiurai, amongst others.

There are a myriad of ways to describe the works in this exhibition, but we have picked eight key adjectives that speak to the variety of objects and ideas in the exhibition. Our glossary below is a guide to some of those related to the themes and concepts explored by artists.

MONOCHROME – often used to describe artworks that are black-and-white, this word comes from mono (one) and chroma (colour) .

SERIAL – in series; similar or even identical individual artworks that come together in succession to form a larger body of work.

QUEER – a reclaimed umbrella term for LGBTQ+ people and other “outsiders” to social norms of gender and sexuality.

POLITICAL – relating to systems of power and social structures like nations, governments, and institutions.

TEXTUAL – using or relating to written language; based on reading and writing words to create meaning.

CAMP – having a deliberately theatrical sensibility; wittily extravagant; “extra”.

UNCANNY – slightly off or odd, and unsettlingly so, being beyond what is normal or expected; strange and mysterious; relates especially to the human figure.

ORGANIC – coming from natural living matter like a plant, an animal, or the soil.

Image Credit : Detail from Frances Goodman, Ophiophilia, 2014. Acrylic nails, glue, polyurethane foam, wire, resin and hessian object, 227 x 315 x 75cm. Zeitz MOCAA Permanent Collection, by kind donation ARTCO Trust (Private Collection).

editorial_excerpt_zh: 图像中的基莎·斯卡维尔：父亲的肖像。艺术家基莎·斯卡维尔对她父亲一张童年护照照片进行了300多次重新加工。她的新书《护照》探讨了父亲的过去、公民身份与身份认同之间的联系，以及黑人散居群体。作者：盖亚·斯夸尔奇（Gaia Squarci）。……

article_text:
Artist Keisha Scarville has reworked a childhood passport photograph of her father more than 300 times. Her book Passports explores his past, the link between citizenship and identity, and the Black diaspora.

By Gaia Squarci. Artwork by Keisha Scarville, courtesy of MACK and the artist.

Through images and fragments of text, the book reads like a dialogue with her father: an attempt to understand him better and, through him, to understand her own roots. It begins with a photograph of him at 16, younger than she ever knew him. The images are altered and collaged, multiplying her father’s identity and connecting his story to the histories of the Black diaspora that began centuries before he was born.

Alongside these portraits, archival photographs taken between the 1960s and 1980s in Guyana and New York City evoke the two places that shaped his life: his native Guyana, which he left as a boy, and New York City, where he later settled. A written conversation with her father traces the steps he took, what he gained and lost along the way, and his sense of belonging to a country where he has spent most of his life.

The book Passports is published by MACK and available for £50.00 GBP.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Patrick Schwarzenegger ( The White Lotus ) will star as a down-on-his-luck tennis pro who is drawn into the dark world of match-fixing to make ends meet for his family in crime-thriller The Journeyman .

Leslie Grace ( In the Heights ) will co-star as his fiercely loyal fiancée. Ángel Manuel Soto ( Wrecking Crew ) will direct from a script by husband-wife duo The Roberts with revisions by Bill Dubuque ( Ozark ).

AGC Studios will fully finance and produce the crime-thriller. Stuart Ford will produce alongside Bryan Haas ( The Order ), Mason Eways, and Scott Franklin ( Black Swan ), with AGC’s Miguel A. Palos, Jr., Zach Garrett and Anant Tamirisa executive-producing.

Related Stories

Dylan Douglas' Movie Debut 'The Hit On Hitler' Heads To AFM With Bleiberg, First Look

YA Vampire Adaptation 'House Of Night' Gets New Director, Casting Underway & Shoot Eyed For Early 2027

Pic will begin shooting on November 30th in San Juan, Puerto Rico, with The Pimienta Film Company providing production services.

Watch on Deadline

The White Lotus and Love of Your Life star Schwarzenegger is currently filming Mike Birbiglia’s Focus Features comedy Old Friends New Friend s. In the Heights star Grace recently released album Amor Quien Eres? through Sony Music Latin.

Puerto Rican filmmaker Manuel Soto’s latest feature was the Amazon MGM action-comedy The Wrecking Crew starring Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista. He previously directed Blue Beetle (Warner Bros./DC), the first Latino-led superhero film from a major studio, and Charm City Kings , which premiered at Sundance and won a U.S. Dramatic Special Jury Award for its ensemble cast.

AGC International reps the film’s international rights and will continue shopping the project at next month’s American Film Market. UTA and WME are co-repping domestic sales with AGC.

The film has been in the works a little while and a couple years back had Dev Patel aboard to star with Tarsem Singh directing.

Ángel Manuel Soto is repped by WME and Redefine Entertainment; Patrick Schwarzenegger is repped by UTA, Entertainment 360, and Goodman, Genow; Leslie Grace is repped by CAA and 641 Meridian; The Roberts are repped by Gersh Agency and LBI Entertainment; and Anant Tamirisa is representing AGC Studios.
